title: Any party of six has three mutual friends or three mutual strangers
body: Pick any six people, and however the friendships fall, you can always find three who all know each other or three who are all strangers. The proof is short: take one person, P. Of the other five, at least three are all P’s friends or all strangers to P, by the **pigeonhole principle**. Say three are friends; if any two of them know each other, they plus P are three mutual friends, and if none do, those three are mutual strangers. Five people are not enough: seat them in a pentagon, each knowing only their two neighbours, and no trio appears.

slides.heading: The proof in four moves
items: Pick anyone; call her P. Each of the other five is her friend or a stranger
At least three are in the same group (pigeonhole). Say three friends
If two of those three are friends, they and P are three mutual friends
If no two are, those three are three mutual strangers

slides.heading: Why five won’t do
slides.text: Draw five people as the corners of a pentagon. Let each know only their two neighbours, so the sides are friendships and the star inside is strangers. Every triangle you can pick uses both kinds of line, so there is no trio of friends and no trio of strangers.

slides.heading: Ramsey’s theorem
slides.text: In 1930, in a paper called On a Problem of Formal Logic, Frank Ramsey proved a far more general result: make a structure large enough and some orderly pattern inside it becomes unavoidable. The party puzzle is its simplest case, written R(3,3) = 6.

slides.heading: Guests needed to force a group of friends or a group of strangers
slides.note: Ramsey numbers R(3,3) to R(4,5). R(5,5) is unknown: somewhere from 43 to 46.

slides.question: Which idea makes the first step of the proof work?
slides.explanation: Five people sorted into two boxes, friends and strangers, must put at least three in one box. From there the triangle is forced.
